title: Kerala Seafarer Stranded in Iran Gets Emergency Certificate, Set to Return Home
excerpt: The MEA said Akshay Harish, disembarked at Chabahar Port after his passport and seafarer documents were reported lost, is now ready to travel back to Kerala, while India separately pressed Pakistan over six seafarers stranded at Karachi for six months.
body:
• India's Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday that an emergency certificate has been issued to Akshay Harish, the Kerala seafarer stranded at Iran's Chabahar Port, clearing his return home.
  • Harish was disembarked from the merchant vessel Plan Marine after he was told his passport and Continuous Discharge Certificate had been lost; he first contacted the Indian consulate on November 9.
  • The MEA is coordinating with his employer and the ship's owner so he can travel back to Kerala as early as possible.
  • The case moved fast once the mission was contacted — four days from first contact to travel document — a route families of stranded seafarers can use through Indian missions abroad.

An Indian seafarer stranded in Iran after his passport and discharge papers were reported lost has been issued an emergency travel certificate and is ready to return home, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Friday. Akshay Harish, a native of Prakkulam in Kerala's Kollam district, was disembarked from his vessel at Chabahar Port and had been unable to travel because he held no valid documents.

"Our mission in Tehran and our Consulate in Bandar Abbas has already reached out to this gentleman, Akshay Harish, a seafarer. He contacted our Consulate on 9th November," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a media briefing in New Delhi, according to IANS. Jaiswal said Harish had boarded the merchant vessel Plan Marine in Japan in 2025, and when the ship reached Chabahar, "he was informed by the captain that his passport and CDC certificate — that is, the Continuous Discharge Certificate which all seafarers or mariners hold — these documents were lost, and therefore he was disembarked from the vessel."

"He applied for an emergency certificate and now that emergency certificate has been issued to Mr. Akshay. With that, now he is ready to travel back home and we are making all efforts so that he can return home to India, to Kerala, as early as possible."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

How he ended up stranded

Harish joined the shipping company in December 2025 through a recruiting agency based in Palakkad, according to ANI's reporting of the case. Earlier coverage described how the vessel's crew documents had gone missing after port proceedings abroad, leaving him confined at Chabahar while other crew members were repatriated through their own embassies. His mother appealed to local and national leaders for help, and the case was taken up with the Iranian authorities as well as the Indian Embassy in Tehran.

Jaiswal said Harish's company is supporting him with boarding and lodging, and that the mission has been in touch with the ship's owner and agent to complete the formalities for his documentation. "In this regard, we are in close contact with his employer," he said.

Six more seafarers stranded at Karachi

The briefing also covered a second, longer-running case. India has made a formal consular request to Pakistan and is engaging with shipping operators over six Indian seafarers who have been stranded aboard a vessel at Karachi Port for more than six months. Jaiswal said the delay stems from an employment and crewing dispute between the sailors and the ship's owner, and that maritime regulations prevent crew members from disembarking until a replacement team arrives.

India's merchant navy workforce is one of the largest in the world, and cases of seafarers stranded by lost documents, unpaid wages or owner disputes surface regularly across West Asian ports. The MEA's account of the Harish case underlines the first step that worked: direct contact with the nearest Indian mission, which triggered consular outreach, employer engagement and the emergency certificate within days.

What happens next

With the emergency certificate issued, the remaining steps are travel arrangements, which the MEA says are being worked out with the employer so Harish can return to Kerala at the earliest. The Karachi case has no such timeline yet: it depends on resolving the crewing dispute that is keeping the six sailors aboard their vessel.
